01.note: Some hooligans in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood caused him a great deal of anguish, and he prayed that they would die. His wife Berurya challenged him: the verse he relied on says "Let sins cease from the land", not sinners, and it ends "and the wicked will be no more", which can only mean the wicked stop being wicked. Pray instead, she told him, that they repent. Rabbi Meir prayed for mercy on them, and they repented.
01.why: The discussion has been reading the opening psalms and David's attitude to the wicked. Berurya's reading turns a verse about the end of the wicked into a hope for their repentance, and the Gemara goes on to another example of her sharp reading of scripture.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage troubled by hooligans in his neighborhood, who first prays for their death.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: Rabbi Meir's wife, who corrects his reading of the verse.

02.note: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya were dining together, Rabbi Yishmael reclining and Rabbi Elazar sitting upright. When the time for the evening Shema came, Rabbi Elazar reclined and Rabbi Yishmael sat up. Rabbi Elazar took offense and told a parable of a man who grows his beard only to spite those who shave: whatever I do, you do the opposite. Rabbi Yishmael answered that he had acted as Beit Hillel rule and Rabbi Elazar as Beit Shammai rule, and that he feared the students would see Rabbi Elazar and fix the law that way for generations.
02.why: A baraita reports Beit Hillel's ruling that Shema may be said in any position, and brings this incident to show it in practice. The Gemara then asks why Rabbi Yishmael needed his second reason, the fear about the students.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who sits up for the evening Shema to show it need not be said reclining.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Rabbi Yishmael's dining companion, who reclines for Shema and is offended when Rabbi Yishmael sits up.

terms.meaning: The declaration of faith beginning "Hear, O Israel", which Jews recite every evening and morning.
Two early schools of Sages who disagree on many rulings. The law usually follows Beit Hillel.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law.

03.note: Beit Hillel told Beit Shammai of a time when the elders of both schools visited Rabbi Yoḥanan ben HaḤoranit during Sukkot. They found him with his head and most of his body inside the sukka and his table inside the house, and, Beit Hillel said, no one said a word to him. Beit Shammai replied that this proves nothing: the elders did tell him that if this was his habit, he had never in his life fulfilled the mitzva of sukka.
03.why: Rav Yosef holds that one who follows Beit Shammai on Shema has done nothing at all. He cites this dispute: Beit Shammai held that someone who ignored their ruling had not fulfilled the mitzva, and since the law follows Beit Hillel, the same applies to those who follow Beit Shammai.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben HaḤoranit
people.about: The man the elders of both schools visited, found sitting partly outside his sukka.

terms.meaning: The temporary hut in which Jews eat and live during the festival of Sukkot.
A commandment of the Torah or of the Sages.
Two early schools of Sages who disagree on many rulings. The law usually follows Beit Hillel.

04.note: Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yosei bar Abba happened to visit a certain place, and the people there asked them what the "single blessing" in a certain mishna was. They had no answer ready. They went and asked Rav Mattana, who also had no answer. Then they asked Rav Yehuda, who told them that Shmuel said it was the blessing "An abounding love".
04.why: A mishna about the Temple says the priests on duty were told to recite a single blessing before Shema, without naming it. This story answers which one; the Gemara then brings Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's view that it was "Who creates light".

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage asked about the mishna while visiting a certain place.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Abba
people.about: Rabbi Abba's companion on the visit.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: The first Sage they asked, who had no answer.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who gave the answer, in the name of Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose answer Rav Yehuda reports.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.
The opening words, and so the name, of a blessing about God's love for Israel and the gift of Torah, said before the morning Shema.

05.note: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were tying the wedding canopy for Rabbi Elazar. He told them he would go to the study hall in the meantime and bring them back something new. There he heard a teaching recited before Rabbi Yoḥanan: one who erred in Shema and does not know where must go back to the start of the paragraph, or to the first break, or to the first of the two verses about writing. Rabbi Yoḥanan added that if he had already begun "In order to lengthen your days", he can assume he kept to his routine. Rabbi Elazar came back and told them, and they said: Had we come only to hear this, it would have been enough.
05.why: The mishna has just ruled that one who erred in Shema goes back to where he erred. The story supplies the rule for one who does not know where his mistake was.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of the two Sages tying Rabbi Elazar's wedding canopy.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: The other Sage tying the canopy.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The groom, who slips off to the study hall and brings back a teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage in the study hall who adds his comment to the teaching.

terms.meaning: The declaration of faith beginning "Hear, O Israel", which Jews recite every evening and morning.
Here, a man in the study hall whose job was to memorize and recite teachings word for word.

06.note: When Rabbi Eliezer's maidservant died, his students came to comfort him. He went up to the upper floor, then into the gatehouse, then into the banquet hall, and they followed him each time. He said: I thought a hint, like lukewarm water, would be enough to burn you; now you are not burned even by boiling water. Did I not teach you that for slaves and maidservants there is no row of comforters and no mourners' blessing or consolation? Instead one says, as for a man whose ox or donkey died: May the Omnipresent replenish your loss.
06.why: The mishna said Rabban Gamliel accepted condolences when his servant Tavi died. A baraita rules that one does not formally comfort mourners for slaves, and this story shows Rabbi Eliezer applying that rule.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose maidservant died, who refuses his students' condolences.

terms.meaning: Comforters stood in a line so the mourners could pass between them and be consoled.
A name for God.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law.

07.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Yonatan were walking in a cemetery, and the sky-blue string of Rabbi Yonatan's ritual fringes was dragging over the graves. Rabbi Ḥiyya told him to lift it, so the dead would not say: Tomorrow they will join us, and now they insult us. Rabbi Yonatan asked whether the dead know so much, since scripture says "the dead know nothing". Rabbi Ḥiyya told him he had not studied the verse properly: "the living" who know they will die are the righteous, who are called living even in death, like Benayahu son of Yehoyada, "son of a living man". The text does not say whether Rabbi Yonatan lifted the string.
07.why: The discussion has been about the respect owed to the dead, such as escorting a funeral. This exchange opens the question the Gemara pursues next: do the dead know what happens among the living?

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage who tells his companion not to insult the dead with his dragging fringes.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: Rabbi Ḥiyya's companion, who doubts the dead know anything.

terms.meaning: Strings tied to the corners of a garment as the Torah commands; one string was dyed sky-blue.

08.note: After Rabbi Ḥiyya's death, his sons went out to the villages and forgot what they had learned, and struggled to remember it. One said to the other: Does our father know of our anguish? The other answered: How would he know? It is written, "His sons are honored yet he shall not know it." The account breaks off here; the reply to this comes in the discussion that follows.
08.why: The Gemara has been debating whether the dead know what happens among the living, and has read "the dead know nothing" as referring to the wicked. The brothers' exchange carries that question on.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The brothers' late father, whom they wonder about.

08.flag: The STORY ends mid-dialogue: the first brother's rebuttal and their conclusion (dead know their own pain, not others') are in the AFTER segments.

09.note: In a drought year a pious man gave a poor man a dinar on the eve of Rosh HaShana. His wife mocked him, and he went and slept in the cemetery. He heard two spirits talking: one could not roam because she was buried in a mat of reeds, so the other went and heard from behind the heavenly curtain that hail would strike crops sown in the first rainy season. He sowed in the second, and only his crops were spared. The next year he heard that blight would strike the second sowing, sowed in the first, and was spared again. His wife asked why and he told her. Soon she quarreled with the dead girl's mother and taunted her that her daughter was buried in reeds. The next year the spirits said: our words have been heard among the living.
09.why: The Gemara had concluded that the dead know their own pain but not that of others. This teaching is raised as a challenge, since the spirits knew what was said among the living; the Gemara answers that perhaps someone who died told them.

terms.meaning: The curtain that separates God's presence from the world; what is heard behind it is what has been decided in heaven.
The Jewish New Year, when the coming year is judged.
The rains of autumn came in stages; farmers chose which stage to sow in.

10.note: Ze'iri used to leave his money with his innkeeper, a woman. While he was going back and forth to the school of Rav, she died. He went after her to the cemetery and asked her where the money was. She told him to get it from beneath the door hinge in a certain place, and to tell her mother to send her comb and her tube of eyeshadow with a certain woman who would be coming there the next day.
10.why: The Gemara is testing whether the dead know what happens among the living, and brings this as a proof: she knew who would die tomorrow. It rejects the proof, suggesting the angel Duma, who watches over the dead, announces arrivals in advance.

people.name: Ze'iri
people.about: A Sage who goes to the grave of his innkeeper to ask where his money is.

terms.meaning: The study house of the Sage Rav, where Ze'iri was going to learn.

11.note: Orphans' money had been left with Shmuel's father, who died while Shmuel was away, so people called Shmuel the son of one who eats orphans' money. Shmuel went to the cemetery and asked the dead for Abba bar Abba, father of Shmuel, and was told he had gone up to the yeshiva on high. Shmuel saw his friend Levi sitting outside, barred for having upset Rabbi Afes by not attending his yeshiva. His father came, crying because Shmuel would soon join him and laughing because Shmuel was very important in this world. Shmuel said: if I am important, let them admit Levi, and they did. His father told him the money was in the millhouse, his own on top and bottom and the orphans' in the middle, so thieves or the earth would take his own first.
11.why: Another proof that the dead know what happens among the living: Shmuel's father knew his son would soon die. The Gemara answers that Shmuel may be different, since for so important a man they announce in advance to make room.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The son, accused of keeping orphans' money, who goes to the cemetery to ask his dead father.

people.name: Abba bar Abba
people.about: Shmuel's father, who had held the orphans' money.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Shmuel's friend, kept outside the heavenly yeshiva until Shmuel speaks for him.

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: The head of a yeshiva whom Levi upset by not attending it.

terms.meaning: The academy in heaven where, in the Gemara's stories, the righteous dead study Torah.

12.note: Rav Pappa reported that after Mar Shmuel died, someone spoke disparagingly about him, and a reed fell from the ceiling and fractured his skull.
12.why: Rabbi Yitzḥak said speaking ill of the dead is like speaking about a stone, because the dead either do not know or do not care. This report challenges that; the Gemara answers that a Torah scholar is different, because God Himself upholds his honor.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who was spoken of disparagingly after his death.

13.note: Rabbi Yehuda insisted that Akavya ben Mahalalel was never ostracized, God forbid, since no one in all Israel matched him in wisdom, purity and fear of sin. The man who was ostracized, he said, was Elazar ben Ḥanokh, who cast doubt on the washing of the hands. When he died, the court sent word and a large stone was placed on his coffin, to teach that when someone dies under a ban, the court stones his coffin.
13.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said the Mishna has twenty-four cases where the court ostracizes someone to defend the honor of a teacher, and Rabbi Elazar found three. This is the source for one of them: one who demeans the washing of the hands.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who denies that Akavya ben Mahalalel was ostracized.

people.name: Akavya ben Mahalalel
people.about: A Sage said in another account to have been ostracized; Rabbi Yehuda says no one matched his wisdom and purity.

people.name: Elazar ben Ḥanokh
people.about: The man Rabbi Yehuda says was ostracized, for doubting the washing of the hands.

terms.meaning: A ban imposed by a court: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
A ritual washing of the hands instituted by the Sages.

14.note: Ḥoni HaMe'aggel, the circle-drawer, drew a circle, stood inside it and said he would not leave until it rained, even making demands about how the rain should fall. After the rain came, Shimon ben Shataḥ sent him word: You deserve to be ostracized, and if you were not Ḥoni I would ostracize you. But what can I do? You nag God and He does your bidding, like a son who nags his father and gets his way. About you scripture says: "Your father and mother will be glad, and she who bore you will rejoice."
14.why: The Gemara is listing the Mishna's cases where the court ostracizes to defend honor. This is its source for the third case Rabbi Elazar found: one who is arrogant toward Heaven would ordinarily deserve the ban.

people.name: Ḥoni HaMe'aggel
people.about: The circle-drawer, who would not leave his circle until God sent rain.

people.name: Shimon ben Shataḥ
people.about: The head of the Sanhedrin, who says Ḥoni deserves a ban but cannot impose it.

terms.meaning: A ban imposed by a court: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
The high court of the Sages.

15.note: Theodosius of Rome, a leader of the Jews there, started a custom for them to eat whole roasted young goats on the eve of Passover, as was done with the Passover lamb in the Temple. Shimon ben Shataḥ sent him word: If you were not Theodosius, I would ostracize you, because you are feeding Israel consecrated food outside the Temple.
15.why: After finding three ostracism cases, the Gemara asks whether there are more, and raises this one. It answers that this case does not count, because it comes from a baraita, not from the Mishna that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was counting.

people.name: Theodosius of Rome
people.about: The leader of the Jews of Rome, who began the custom of roasted goats on Passover eve.

people.name: Shimon ben Shataḥ
people.about: The Sage who warns Theodosius he would ban him if he were not so important.

terms.meaning: A ban imposed by a court: the person is shunned by the community until the ban is lifted.
Food from sacrifices, which may be eaten only at the Temple; roasting goats like the Passover lamb looked like eating sacrifices elsewhere.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law.

16.note: Rav Adda bar Ahava saw a woman in the market wearing a garment of wool and linen woven together, which the Torah forbids. Thinking she was Jewish, he ripped it off her. She turned out not to be Jewish, and the payment for her shame was set at four hundred zuz. He asked her name, and she said Matun. He said, punning on matan, the Aramaic for two hundred: Matun, matun, is worth four hundred zuz.
16.why: Rav Pappa asked Abaye why miracles happened for earlier generations and not for theirs, though they studied more. Abaye answered that the earlier Sages gave themselves wholly for the sanctification of God's name, and this incident shows that zeal.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage who tears a forbidden garment off a woman he thinks is Jewish.

people.name: Matun
people.about: The woman whose garment he tore; she was not Jewish.

terms.meaning: A silver coin.

17.note: Rabbi Yehuda had had a seminal emission and was walking along the riverbank with his disciples. They asked him to teach them a chapter of Hilkhot Derekh Eretz. He went down into the river, immersed, and taught them. They said: Did you not teach us that one may study Hilkhot Derekh Eretz in that state? He answered: Although I am lenient with others, I am strict with myself.
17.why: The Sages barred a man who had a seminal emission from studying Torah, and Sages disagree how far the ban reaches. Rabbi Yehuda allows only Hilkhot Derekh Eretz; the story shows him holding himself to more than his own ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who immerses before teaching, though his own ruling did not require it.

terms.meaning: Under a rule of the Sages, a man who has had a seminal emission is ritually impure and may not study Torah until he purifies himself with water.
Teachings on proper conduct and manners.
Dipped his whole body in natural water to become ritually pure.

18.note: A student was reciting hesitantly before Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira; the translation explains that he had had a seminal emission and did not want to say words of Torah plainly. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira told him: My son, open your mouth and let your words shine, for words of Torah do not become impure. As scripture says, "Is not my word like fire, says the Lord": just as fire does not become impure, words of Torah do not become impure.
18.why: The discussion is about how much Torah a man may study after a seminal emission. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira allows all of it, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak later says common practice follows him on this.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: The Sage who tells a hesitant student that Torah cannot become impure.

terms.meaning: Under a rule of the Sages, a man who has had a seminal emission is ritually impure and may not study Torah until he purifies himself with water.
In a state of ritual impurity, which bars a person or object from certain holy things until purified.

19.note: A man tried to persuade a woman to sin with him. She said to him: Good-for-nothing! Do you have forty se'a of water to immerse yourself in afterwards? He immediately gave up.
19.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked why one needs a full immersion of forty se'a when nine kav poured over a person might do. Rabbi Ḥanina answers that the demanding rule is a great fence against sin, and cites this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage who cites this incident.

terms.meaning: The amount of water a ritual bath must hold; a se'a is a measure of volume. Immersing in it removes impurity, here the impurity after intercourse.

20.note: Rabbi Zeira was sitting in a tub of water in the bathhouse and told his attendant to bring nine kav of water and pour it over him. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba asked why he needed that, since he was already sitting in water. Rabbi Zeira answered that nine kav is like forty se'a: just as forty se'a purifies by immersion and not by pouring, nine kav purifies by pouring and not by immersion.
20.why: The Sages are debating how a man becomes pure after a seminal emission: immersion in forty se'a, in a heated bath, or nine kav poured over him. Rabbi Zeira's act shows how the nine-kav method must be done.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage purifying himself in the bathhouse.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: The Sage who asks Rabbi Zeira why he needs water poured on him.

terms.meaning: A smaller amount of water (a kav is a measure of volume) that, poured over a man, purifies him after a seminal emission.
The amount of water a ritual bath must hold for immersion.
